dilatory

/DIL-uh-tor-ee/ - the stress falls on DIL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Dilatory means tending to delay; slow to act.

The landlord was notoriously dilatory about repairs: tenants learned that a promise of 'next week' meant a month if it meant anything.

Worked Example

The insurance company's dilatory handling of claims was strategy, not sloppiness — adjusters were coached to request one more document each week until exhausted claimants settled for less.

Dilatory is sharper than 'slow': slowness can be innocent, but dilatory behavior tends toward delay — often deliberately — and the word carries a note of blame, which is why courts and referees use it for stalling tactics.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tardy: Tardy means late against a fixed time — the class bell, the 9 a.m. meeting — and it usually describes a single miss. Dilatory describes the habit behind repeated lateness: a settled tendency to delay that earns blame.

sluggish: Sluggish means slow from low energy — cold syrup, a drained battery, a sleepy Monday crew — with no hint of intent. Dilatory carries fault: the dilatory party delays something owed, often on purpose.

dawdling: Dawdling is wasting time in small, aimless ways — poking along, stopping to look at everything. It is childlike where dilatory is accusatory: courts call stalling tactics dilatory, but nobody files a formal complaint about dawdling.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

prompt: acting right away, without delay

brisk: moving at a quick, businesslike pace

Where it sits · how blameworthy the delay is — unhurried → dilatory → obstructive

unhurried vs. dilatory: Unhurried is neutral, even pleasant — a Sunday stroll is unhurried; it stops well short of dilatory, which blames the slowness for delaying something owed.

obstructive vs. dilatory: Obstructive goes further than dilatory: the dilatory party drags its feet, while the obstructive one actively blocks the road.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dilat-

Root — dilat-: put off, deferred (Latin dilatus, 'carried apart')

Suffix — -ory

Suffix — -ory: tending to

Put it together

Put it together: Latin differre meant 'to carry apart — to postpone,' and its past form dilatus gives the stem dilat-. Add -ory, 'tending to,' and dilatory describes whatever tends to postpone. One caution: dilate, 'to widen,' comes from a different Latin word latus meaning 'wide' — the spelling twins are not relatives.

Use the root in a new word: relate

Use the root in a new word: relate: Witnesses were asked to relate the day's events exactly as they remembered them.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Dilatory belongs to formal complaint — audits, rulings, referee reports — where slowness is a fault. For a friend who is simply slow, 'poky' or 'slow' will do; say dilatory when the delay looks like a habit or a tactic and you mean to assign blame.
